references.text: Jesus already prophesied at his entry into Jerusalem that enemies would level the city to the ground and 'not leave one stone upon another' in it, using exactly the same expression (οὐκ ἀφήσουσιν λίθον ἐπὶ λίθον). See [ref:Luk 19:44|Luke 19:44].

The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus predicts the temple's destruction with the words 'not one stone will be left here upon another that will not be thrown down' (οὐ μὴ ἀφεθῇ ὧδε λίθος ἐπὶ λίθον ὃς οὐ καταλυθήσεται). See [ref:Matt 24:1-2|Matthew 24:1-2].

The parallel passage in Mark where the disciples point out the temple's large stones and buildings, and Jesus responds with the same prophecy that not one stone will be left upon another. See [ref:Mark 13:1-2|Mark 13:1-2].

The prophet Micah prophesied that Zion would be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become a heap of ruins, and the temple hill to become wooded hills – a prophecy of total destruction pointing forward to what Jesus predicts here. See [ref:Mi 3:12|Micah 3:12].

Jeremiah prophesied that Zion would be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become a heap of ruins, a parallel to Jesus' prophecy about the temple's complete destruction. See [ref:Jer 26:18|Jeremiah 26:18].
Daniel's prophecy that the city and sanctuary will be destroyed by the people of a coming prince, which points forward to the destruction Jesus predicts here. See [ref:Dan 9:26|Daniel 9:26].

Later in the same discourse, Jesus expands on his prophecy about Jerusalem's destruction, where the city will be surrounded by armies and its people fall by the sword and be taken as captives. See [ref:Luk 21:20-24|Luke 21:20-24].

The Lord warned Solomon that if Israel turned away, the temple would be laid in ruins and become an object of horror, so that all who passed by would be appalled. This principle of God's judgment on the temple is reflected in Jesus' prophecy. See [ref:1 Kong 9:7-8|1 Kings 9:7-8].
